reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight of the paper lies in decomposing corner three-point efficiency into components driven by distance, contest, and generation mechanisms. Efficiency decomposition uses logistic regression to isolate the influence of distance alone, revealing that even after controlling for distance, corner threes remain 4.1 percentage points more efficient than above-the-break threes—a gap not fully explained by distance alone. This suggests that factors like spacing, timing, and shot selection contribute. Trajectory clustering identifies recurring motion patterns in the 4 seconds prior to the shot, enabling classification of offensive setups into distinct behavioral clusters. These clusters inform understanding of how offenses generate corner threes, with high-coherence clusters indicating predictable sequences. The defensive game model treats the interaction between a corner defender and an offense as a zero-sum game, where the defender selects a distance from the shooter and the offense chooses between driving or kicking out. Payoff matrices incorporate both single-defender qSQ data and a double-team model, yielding equilibrium strategies. The Nash equilibrium predicts a defender distance of approximately 13 feet, which aligns closely with empirical observations (12.3 ft), though the shape of the distribution differs—suggesting deviations from rational play. These primitives collectively enable modeling of strategic interactions in basketball and provide methodological frameworks adaptable to NFL NGS analytics.
